title: Chapter 41 — Moby Dick
paragraphs: I, Ishmael, was one of that crew. My shouts had gone up with the rest. My oath had been welded with theirs. And I shouted louder and hammered my oath harder because of the dread in my soul. A wild, mystical, sympathetic feeling was in me. Ahab's unquenchable feud seemed like my own. With eager ears I learned the history of that murderous monster against whom I and all the others had sworn our oaths of violence and revenge.

For some time past, though only at intervals, the solitary, secluded White Whale had haunted those uncivilized seas mostly visited by the Sperm Whale hunters. But not all of them knew of his existence. Only a few, comparatively, had knowingly seen him, and the number who had actually and knowingly fought him was very small indeed. For many reasons — the large number of whale ships; the disorderly way they were scattered over the entire watery globe, many of them adventurously pushing their hunt along lonely latitudes, so that for a whole year or more at a stretch they might seldom or never meet a single sail of any sort that could tell them news; the extreme length of each voyage; the irregular times of sailing from home — all these, with other circumstances direct and indirect, had long prevented the specific news about Moby Dick as an individual from spreading through the whole worldwide whaling fleet. Several ships were reported to have encountered, at such and such a time or on such and such a meridian, a Sperm Whale of unusual size and malignity which, after doing great damage to its attackers, had completely escaped them; it could hardly be doubted — to some minds, I say, it was not an unfair assumption — that this whale must have been none other than Moby Dick. Yet since the Sperm Whale fishery had lately seen various and not infrequent instances of great ferocity, cunning, and malice in the whale under attack, those who by accident unknowingly fought Moby Dick were perhaps, for the most part, content to blame the peculiar terror he inspired more, as it were, on the dangers of the Sperm Whale fishery at large than on the individual cause. That, mostly, was how the disastrous encounter between Ahab and the whale had so far been popularly regarded.

As for those who had previously heard of the White Whale and then happened to see him — at first, almost every one of them had lowered for him as boldly and fearlessly as for any other sperm whale. But eventually, such catastrophes resulted from these attacks — not just sprained wrists and ankles, broken limbs, or devouring amputations, but fatalities of the deadliest kind — that these repeated, disastrous defeats, all piling their terrors onto Moby Dick, had gone far toward shaking the courage of many brave hunters who later heard the story of the White Whale.

Nor did wild rumors of all kinds fail to exaggerate the true accounts of these deadly encounters and make them still more horrifying. For not only do fantastic rumors naturally grow out of the very body of all surprising, terrible events, as a stricken tree gives birth to its fungi, but in life at sea, far more than on dry land, wild rumors abound wherever there is any adequate reality for them to cling to. And just as the sea surpasses the land in this respect, so the whale fishery surpasses every other kind of seafaring life in the wonder and fearfulness of the rumors that sometimes circulate there. For whalemen as a body are not exempt from the ignorance and superstition that all sailors inherit; but of all sailors, they are by far the most directly brought into contact with whatever is appallingly astonishing in the sea. Face to face they not only see its greatest marvels, but, hand to jaw, they fight them. Alone, in waters so remote that you could sail a thousand miles and pass a thousand shores without coming to a single chiseled hearthstone, or anything hospitable beneath that part of the sun — in such latitudes and longitudes, and pursuing such a calling as he does, the whaleman is wrapped in influences that all tend to make his imagination pregnant with many a mighty birth.

No wonder, then, that as the rumors of the White Whale kept gathering bulk from merely crossing the widest ocean spaces, they finally absorbed all manner of morbid hints and half-formed, fetal suggestions of supernatural forces, which in the end invested Moby Dick with new terrors borrowed from nothing that visibly appears. So in many cases he finally struck such a panic that, of those who had heard of the White Whale — through those rumors, at least — few of those hunters were willing to face the dangers of his jaw.

But there were still other, more vital practical influences at work. Even today, the original prestige of the Sperm Whale, as fearfully distinguished from all other species of leviathan, has not died out of the minds of whalemen as a body. There are those among them today who, though intelligent and brave enough to give battle to the Greenland or right whale, would perhaps — from lack of professional experience, or incompetence, or timidity — decline a contest with the Sperm Whale. At any rate, there are plenty of whalemen, especially among the whaling nations not sailing under the American flag, who have never met the Sperm Whale in battle, and whose only knowledge of the leviathan is limited to the ignoble monster originally hunted in the North. Seated on their hatches, these men will listen with a childlike fireside interest and awe to the wild, strange tales of southern whaling. And nowhere is the supreme tremendousness of the great Sperm Whale more deeply felt and understood than aboard the ships whose bows breast him.

And as if the now proven reality of his power had, in earlier legendary times, cast its shadow before it, we find some book naturalists — Olassen and Povelson — declaring the Sperm Whale not only to be a terror to every other creature in the sea but so incredibly ferocious as to be continually thirsting for human blood. Even as late as Cuvier's time, these or very similar impressions had not been erased. For in his Natural History, the Baron himself states that at the sight of the Sperm Whale, all fish (sharks included) are "struck with the most lively terrors," and "often in the precipitancy of their flight dash themselves against the rocks with such violence as to cause instantaneous death." And however much the general experience of the fishery may correct such reports, in their full terribleness — even down to Povelson's bloodthirsty detail — the superstitious belief in them is, in some turns of fortune in their calling, revived in the hunters' minds.

So, overawed by the rumors and portents concerning him, not a few of the fishermen recalled, in connection with Moby Dick, the earlier days of the Sperm Whale fishery, when it was often hard to persuade long-practiced right whalemen to embark on the perils of this new and daring warfare. Such men protested that although other leviathans might be pursued with hope of success, to chase and point a lance at such an apparition as the Sperm Whale was not for mortal man. To attempt it would inevitably mean being torn into a quick eternity. On this point, there are some remarkable documents that may be consulted.

Nevertheless, some there were who, even knowing all this, were ready to chase Moby Dick. And an even greater number, having only heard of him vaguely and at a distance, without specific details of any particular disaster and without the superstitious trappings, were tough enough not to flee from the fight if it came to them.

One of the wild ideas I mentioned, which eventually became linked with the White Whale in superstitious minds, was the eerie notion that Moby Dick was everywhere at once — that he had actually been encountered in opposite latitudes at the very same instant.

Nor, credulous as such minds must have been, was this idea altogether without some faint show of superstitious probability. For since the secrets of the ocean currents have never yet been revealed, even to the most learned research, the hidden ways of the Sperm Whale beneath the surface remain, in great part, unaccountable to his pursuers. From time to time they have given rise to the most curious and contradictory speculations, especially about the mystic means by which, after sounding to a great depth, he transports himself with such vast swiftness to the most widely distant points.

It is well known to both American and English whale ships, and was also placed on authoritative record years ago by Scoresby, that some whales captured far north in the Pacific have been found with the barbs of harpoons thrown in the Greenland seas still in their bodies. Nor can it be denied that in some of these cases it has been declared that the time between the two attacks could not have been very many days. Hence, by inference, some whalemen have believed that the Northwest Passage, so long a problem to man, was never a problem to the whale. So that here, in the real living experience of living men, the wonders told in old times of the inland Strello mountain in Portugal (near whose top there was said to be a lake in which the wrecks of ships floated up to the surface), and that still more wonderful story of the Arethusa fountain near Syracuse (whose waters were believed to have come from the Holy Land by an underground passage) — these fabulous tales are almost fully equaled by the realities of the whalemen.

Forced into familiarity with such wonders, then, and knowing that after repeated, fearless attacks the White Whale had escaped alive, it can hardly be surprising that some whalemen went still further in their superstitions. They declared Moby Dick not only everywhere at once but immortal (for immortality is only being everywhere in time). Though groves of spears should be planted in his flanks, he would still swim away unharmed. Or if indeed he should ever be made to spout thick blood, that sight would be only a ghastly deception. For again, in unbloodied waves hundreds of leagues away, his unstained spout would be seen once more.

But even stripped of these supernatural rumors, there was enough in the earthly reality and undeniable character of the monster to strike the imagination with extraordinary power. It was not so much his uncommon size that distinguished him from other sperm whales, but — as mentioned elsewhere — a peculiar snow-white, wrinkled forehead and a high, pyramid-shaped white hump. These were his prominent features, the marks by which, even in the limitless, uncharted seas, he revealed his identity at a great distance to those who knew him.

The rest of his body was so streaked, spotted, and marbled with the same ghostly hue that he had earned his distinctive name of the White Whale. A name literally justified by his vivid appearance when seen gliding at high noon through a dark blue sea, leaving a milky-way wake of creamy foam, all sparkling with golden gleams.

It was not his unusual size, nor his remarkable color, nor even his deformed lower jaw that invested the whale with such natural terror, but rather an unprecedented, intelligent malice that, according to specific accounts, he had displayed over and over in his attacks. Most of all, his treacherous retreats struck more fear than perhaps anything else. For when swimming ahead of his triumphant pursuers, showing every sign of alarm, he had been known several times to turn around suddenly and, bearing down on them, either smash their boats to splinters or drive them back in panic to their ship.

Several deaths had already attended his chase. Though similar disasters, however little talked about on shore, were by no means unusual in the fishery, in most cases the White Whale's ferocity seemed so infernal and premeditated that every maiming or death he caused was not wholly regarded as the work of an unintelligent agent.

Judge, then, what heights of inflamed, frantic fury the minds of his more desperate hunters were driven to when, among the splinters of chewed-up boats and the sinking limbs of torn-apart comrades, they swam out of the white curds of the whale's terrible wrath into the calm, infuriating sunlight, which went on smiling as if at a birth or a wedding.

His three boats stove in around him, and oars and men both whirling in the eddies, one captain had seized the line-knife from his broken bow and dashed at the whale like an Arkansas duelist at his enemy, blindly trying with a six-inch blade to reach the fathom-deep life of the whale. That captain was Ahab. And then it was that Moby Dick, suddenly sweeping his sickle-shaped lower jaw beneath him, reaped away Ahab's leg as a mower cuts a blade of grass in the field. No turbaned Turk, no hired Venetian or Malay, could have struck him with more apparent malice. There was little reason to doubt, then, that ever since that nearly fatal encounter, Ahab had nursed a wild vindictiveness against the whale — all the more deadly because in his frantic morbidness he at last came to identify with him not only all his bodily woes but all his intellectual and spiritual torments. The White Whale swam before him as the monomaniac incarnation of all those malicious forces that some deep men feel eating away inside them, until they are left living on with half a heart and half a lung. That intangible malignity which has existed from the beginning — to whose rule even modern Christians assign one half of the worlds, and which the ancient Ophites of the East revered in their statue devil — Ahab did not fall down and worship it as they did. Instead, deliriously transferring its idea to the hated white whale, he pitted himself, all mutilated, against it. All that most maddens and torments, all that stirs up the dregs of things, all truth with malice in it, all that cracks the sinews and cakes the brain, all the subtle demonisms of life and thought — all evil, to crazy Ahab, was visibly personified and made practically assailable in Moby Dick. He piled upon the whale's white hump the sum of all the general rage and hate felt by his whole race from Adam down. And then, as if his chest had been a mortar, he burst his hot heart's shell upon it.

It is not probable that this monomania in him arose at the precise moment of his bodily dismemberment. Then, in darting at the monster, knife in hand, he had only given way to a sudden, passionate, physical animosity. And when he received the stroke that tore him, he probably felt only the agonizing bodily laceration, and nothing more. Yet when, forced by this collision to turn toward home, Ahab and anguish lay stretched together in one hammock for long months of days and weeks, rounding in midwinter that dreary, howling Patagonian Cape — then it was that his torn body and gashed soul bled into one another, and, so mingling, made him mad. That it was only then, on the homeward voyage after the encounter, that the final monomania seized him seems all but certain from the fact that at intervals during the passage he was a raving lunatic. And though he had lost a leg, such vital strength still lurked in his Egyptian chest, further intensified by his delirium, that his mates were forced to lash him fast, even there, as he sailed, raving in his hammock. In a straitjacket he swung to the mad rocking of the gales. And when, running into more bearable latitudes, the ship floated across the tranquil tropics with mild studding sails spread, and to all appearances the old man's delirium seemed left behind him with the Cape Horn swells, and he came out of his dark den into the blessed light and air — even then, when he showed that firm, collected face, however pale, and gave his calm orders once again, and his mates thanked God the dreadful madness was now gone — even then, Ahab, in his hidden self, raved on. Human madness is often a cunning and most catlike thing. When you think it has fled, it may only have been transfigured into some still subtler form. Ahab's full lunacy did not subside but contracted and deepened, like the undiminished Hudson when that noble Northman flows narrowly but unfathomably through the Highland gorge. And just as in his narrow-flowing monomania not one jot of Ahab's broad madness had been left behind, so in that broad madness not one jot of his great natural intellect had perished. What had been the living agent now became the living instrument. If such a violent figure of speech may stand, his special lunacy stormed his general sanity and carried it, and turned all its concentrated cannon on its own mad target. So far from having lost his strength, Ahab, for that one end, now possessed a thousand times more power than he had ever sanely brought to bear on any one reasonable object.

This is much; yet Ahab's larger, darker, deeper part remains not even hinted at. But it is vain to popularize profundities, and all truth is profound. Winding far down from within the very heart of this spiked Hotel de Cluny where we now stand — however grand and wonderful, leave it now — take your way, you nobler, sadder souls, to those vast Roman halls of the Thermes (the ancient baths beneath it), where far below the fantastic towers of man's upper earth, his root of grandeur, his whole awful essence sits in bearded state: an antique buried beneath antiquities, and throned on torsos! So, with a broken throne, the great gods mock that captive king; so, like a Caryatid (a carved figure serving as a column), he sits patiently, holding up on his frozen brow the piled entablatures of ages. Wind your way down there, you prouder, sadder souls! Question that proud, sad king! A family likeness! Yes, he begat you, you young exiled royalties; and from your grim father alone will the old state secret come.

Now, in his heart, Ahab had some glimpse of this — namely: all my means are sane, my motive and my object mad. Yet without power to kill, change, or escape the fact, he also knew that he had long been deceiving mankind about it — and in some ways still was. But his deception was only subject to his awareness, not to his deliberate will. Nevertheless, he succeeded so well in it that when he stepped ashore on his ivory leg at last, no Nantucketer thought him anything other than naturally grief-stricken, and deeply so, by the terrible accident that had befallen him.

The reports of his undeniable delirium at sea were likewise popularly put down to a related cause. And so too was all the added moodiness that always afterward, right up to the day of sailing in the Pequod on the present voyage, sat brooding on his brow. And it is not so very unlikely that, far from doubting his fitness for another whaling voyage because of such dark symptoms, the calculating people of that prudent island were inclined to entertain the notion that for those very reasons he was all the better qualified and set on edge for a pursuit so full of rage and wildness as the bloody hunt of whales. Gnawed within and scorched without by the fixed, unrelenting fangs of some incurable idea — such a man, if he could be found, would seem the very man to dart his iron and lift his lance against the most appalling of all brutes. Or, if for any reason he were thought physically unfit for that, such a man would seem supremely qualified to cheer and howl his underlings on to the attack. But be all this as it may, this much is certain: with the mad secret of his unabated rage bolted up and locked inside him, Ahab had deliberately sailed on the present voyage with the one sole, all-consuming object of hunting the White Whale. Had any one of his old acquaintances on shore even half dreamed of what was lurking in him then, how quickly their aghast and righteous souls would have wrenched the ship from such a fiendish man! They were bent on profitable cruises, the profit to be counted down in dollars from the mint. He was intent on an audacious, implacable, and supernatural revenge.

Here, then, was this gray-headed, ungodly old man, chasing with curses a Job's whale around the world, at the head of a crew, too, made up chiefly of mongrel renegades, and castaways, and cannibals — a crew morally weakened as well by the helplessness of mere unaided virtue or right-mindedness in Starbuck, the invulnerable jollity of indifference and recklessness in Stubb, and the pervading mediocrity in Flask. Such a crew, so officered, seemed specially picked and packed by some infernal fate to help him to his monomaniac revenge. How it was that they responded so abundantly to the old man's fury — by what evil magic their souls were possessed, so that at times his hate seemed almost theirs, and the White Whale as much their unbearable enemy as his — how all this came to be — what the White Whale was to them, or how, to their unconscious understandings as well, in some dim, unsuspected way, he might have seemed the gliding great demon of the seas of life — to explain all this would be to dive deeper than Ishmael can go. The subterranean miner that works in all of us — how can anyone tell where his shaft leads by the ever-shifting, muffled sound of his pick? Who does not feel the irresistible arm drag? What skiff in tow of a seventy-four (a seventy-four-gun ship of the line) can stand still? For my part, I gave myself up to the abandon of the time and the place. But while still all in a rush to encounter the whale, I could see nothing in that brute but the deadliest ill.
